Method. Elemental cross sections are log-log linearly interpolated on the native NIST XCOM energy grid (1 keV–100 GeV, Z=1–100), which is itself densified around absorption edges specifically so that this interpolation scheme reproduces the tabulated physics accurately. Mass attenuation coefficients are obtained via μ/ρ = σ[barn]·NA·10−24/A[g·mol⁻¹]. Compounds and mixtures combine elemental μ/ρ values as a mass-fraction–weighted sum, matching XCOM's own combination rule. Verified against published reference values (e.g. H₂O: 0.07072 cm²/g at 1 MeV, 0.02219 cm²/g at 10 MeV; H: 0.1263 cm²/g at 1 MeV; Pb: 0.07102 cm²/g at 1 MeV).

Mixture presets approx use representative ICRU-44 / NIST reference compositions and should not be treated as certified values for a specific sample — edit the weight fractions for your actual material. Compound presets exact are exact stoichiometric formulas.

Formula syntax follows XCOM convention: no parentheses, dots, or spaces — subscripts written inline (Ca3P2O8, not Ca3(PO4)2).

1 Overview

This Theory tab documents the physics actually used by the Explorer, Shielding, Shield 2D, Compare, Edges, and NIST Table 4 features. The elemental attenuation data are based on NIST XCOM over 1 keV–100 GeV for Z = 1–100; the bundled NIST SRD 126 Table 4 data cover the directly tabulated compounds and mixtures in their supplied energy range ( NIST X-Ray Mass Attenuation Coefficients ). Photon energy is denoted E throughout — the application accepts input in eV, keV, or MeV and works internally in eV — and Z, A denote an element's atomic number and atomic mass (g/mol).

The five photon-interaction channels used for attenuation are coherent scattering, incoherent (Compton) scattering, photoelectric absorption, nuclear-field pair production, and electron-field pair production. Their contributions form the total attenuation cross section, with the atomic cross section for a channel denoted σ (cm²/atom):

$$\sigma_{\rm tot}=\sigma_{\rm coh}+\sigma_{\rm incoh}+\sigma_{\rm pe}+\kappa_{\rm nuc}+\kappa_e.$$

The coherent, incoherent, and photoelectric contributions are denoted σcoh, σincoh, and σpe; the two pair-production contributions are conventionally denoted κ rather than σ, with κnuc and κe for the nuclear-field and electron-field (triplet) channels respectively. The application then converts these tabulated quantities to mass and linear attenuation coefficients, applies the appropriate material-combination rule, and evaluates transmission through one or more shielding layers.

How to read this page
Each section states the exact formula the application evaluates, in the same symbols the application uses on screen. Every symbol is introduced at the point it first appears, in the same equation or the sentence right before it — refer back to that section instead of re-deriving a symbol's meaning from elsewhere. Cyan terms in the running text are formula symbols; hover-free, they are simply typeset to match the equations.

2 Photon Attenuation & Beer–Lambert Law

The mass attenuation coefficient μ/ρ (cm²/g) is related to the atomic cross section σ (cm²/atom, per channel or summed) by

$$\frac{\mu}{\rho}=\sigma\frac{N_A}{A}.$$

With density ρ (g/cm³) and NA = 6.02214076×1023 mol−1 (Avogadro's number), A the atomic mass (g/mol), the linear attenuation coefficient μ (cm−1) is

$$\mu=\left(\frac{\mu}{\rho}\right)\rho.$$

For a monoenergetic narrow beam crossing a normal (perpendicular) thickness x (cm),

$$T=\frac{I}{I_0}=e^{-\mu x}.$$

Here T is the transmission — the fraction of incident intensity I0 that survives as I, dimensionless, 0–1. The quantity 1/μ is the mean free path. This expression describes the uncollided primary beam; it does not by itself transport photons that have scattered and later reach a detector.

3 Coherent (Rayleigh) Scattering

Coherent scattering is elastic scattering by the bound electron cloud. The photon changes direction with negligible energy loss. The angular dependence can be represented by the Thomson distribution multiplied by an atomic form factor:

$$\frac{d\sigma_{\rm coh}}{d\Omega}=r_e^2\frac{1+\cos^2\theta}{2}[F(q,Z)]^2.$$

Here re is the classical electron radius (the Thomson-scattering constant), θ the scattering angle, and F(q,Z) the atomic form factor modifying the Thomson coherent-scattering distribution. It is strongest at lower energies and for higher-Z materials and is included in the XCOM total attenuation data even though it does not represent photon-energy deposition by itself.

4 Incoherent (Compton) Scattering

The free-electron limit is described by the Klein–Nishina formula. For an incident photon of energy E scattered through angle θ, the scattered photon energy E′ is

$$E'=\frac{E}{1+\dfrac{E}{m_ec^2}(1-\cos\theta)}.$$

Here mec² = 0.511 MeV is the electron rest-mass energy; it sets this formula's scale and the 2mec² / 4mec² pair-production thresholds used later. For bound atomic electrons, the incoherent scattering function modifies the free-electron result. Compton scattering transfers part of the photon energy to an electron and produces a population of scattered photons that can contribute to broad-beam detector response.

5 Photoelectric Absorption

In photoelectric absorption the photon is completely absorbed and a bound electron is ejected. Away from absorption edges the cross section falls rapidly with energy and has a strong Z dependence, approximately of the form

$$\sigma_{\rm pe}\propto\frac{Z^n}{E^m},\qquad n\sim4\!\text{--}\!5,\quad m\sim3\!\text{--}\!3.5.$$

The resulting atomic vacancy can produce characteristic X-rays or Auger electrons. This is the main mechanism behind K-edge-related secondary-photon behavior in high-Z shielding materials.

6 Pair Production

Pair production becomes possible when

$$E\ge 2m_ec^2=1.022007\ {\rm MeV}.$$
  • Nuclear-field pair production: recoil is taken by the nucleus.
  • Electron-field pair production (triplet production): recoil is taken by an atomic electron and the threshold is 4mec2 = 2.044014 MeV.

At high energy the nuclear-field contribution generally dominates in high-Z materials. The generated positron can subsequently annihilate and produce 511-keV photons.

7 Compounds & Mixtures

For elemental mass fractions wi, the app uses the XCOM mass-fraction combination rule

$$\left(\frac{\mu}{\rho}\right)_{\rm mix}=\sum_iw_i\left(\frac{\mu}{\rho}\right)_i.$$

For an exact chemical formula, the elemental fractions are obtained from stoichiometry. User-entered mixture weights are normalized automatically. Preset mixtures use representative reference compositions and should not be treated as certified measurements of a particular sample.

8 Material Parameters: Zeff, Aeff, Zeff(E), Neff & I

The Shielding Material parameters card reports composition and attenuation descriptors for the selected material. These effective-composition quantities are deliberately separated because they answer different questions.

Composition-only effective atomic number. The displayed Zeff uses the electron-fraction convention with exponent p = 2.94:

$$Z_{\rm eff}=\left(\sum_i f_i Z_i^{2.94}\right)^{1/2.94},\qquad f_i=\frac{n_i Z_i}{\sum_j n_j Z_j}.$$

Here ni is the stoichiometric number of atoms of element i. For a pure element, Zeff = Z. For water, H2O, this convention gives approximately Zeff = 7.42.

Effective atomic mass. Aeff is reported using the same electron-fraction weights:

$$A_{\rm eff}=\sum_i f_i A_i.$$

Energy-dependent effective atomic number. Zeff(E) uses the current photon energy and the same elemental XCOM mass-attenuation data used by the shielding calculation. First form the attenuation contribution

$$C_i(E)=w_i\left[\frac{\mu}{\rho}\right]_i(E),\qquad q_i(E)=\frac{C_i(E)}{\sum_j C_j(E)}.$$

The application then evaluates

$$Z_{\rm eff}(E)=\left(\sum_i q_i(E)Z_i^{2.94}\right)^{1/2.94}.$$

Therefore Zeff(E) can change when photon energy changes, especially when the elemental attenuation contributions have different energy dependences or when an absorption edge is crossed. For a pure element it remains equal to that element's Z.

Effective electron density. The material-parameters card also reports Neff, the number of electrons per unit volume implied by the composition-only Zeff and Aeff above:

$$N_{\rm eff}=\rho\,\frac{N_A}{A_{\rm eff}}\,Z_{\rm eff}.$$

Here NA is Avogadro's number (6.02214076×1023 mol−1) and ρ is the material density in g/cm3, so Neff comes out in electrons/cm3. Because it is built from the composition-only Zeff and Aeff rather than Zeff(E), Neff is a fixed property of the material and does not change with photon energy. It is a descriptive quantity for comparing the electron content per unit volume of different materials (relevant to Compton-dominated regimes) and, like Zeff and Aeff, plays no role in the μ/ρ, μ, or transmission calculations themselves.

Mean excitation energy. The card also reports I, the mean excitation energy used in the Bethe stopping-power formula for charged-particle energy loss. Each element in the app's periodic-table data has a fixed Ii value (in eV), taken directly from the ICRU Report 37 recommended values and stored in this application's ELEMENT_MEAN_EXCITATION_EV lookup table (see §29 for the full reference). Unlike every other quantity on this page, I is not derived from the bundled NIST XCOM/SRD-126 photon (x-ray/gamma) data — it is a charged-particle stopping-power quantity (the same I used in electron/proton/alpha Bethe-formula calculations, e.g. by NIST's ESTAR/ASTAR/PSTAR databases) added here purely for convenience. For a compound or mixture the application combines the elemental values with Bragg's additivity rule, weighting each element by its share of the material's electrons per gram, wiZi/Ai:

$$\ln I=\frac{\sum_i w_i\dfrac{Z_i}{A_i}\ln I_i}{\sum_i w_i\dfrac{Z_i}{A_i}}.$$

Here wi is element i's mass fraction in the current material (the same composition used for Zeff(E) above), and the sum runs over the material's constituent elements. For a pure element this reduces to that element's tabulated Ii. Because it depends only on composition, I is a fixed material property like Zeff, Aeff, and Neff — it does not vary with photon energy, and it is unrelated to the photon-attenuation channels (photoelectric, Compton, pair production) that XCOM tabulates; it characterizes charged-particle (electron/proton/alpha) stopping power rather than photon attenuation, and is provided here as a convenience for users who also need it for CSDA-range or stopping-power estimates alongside the photon-shielding results.

Important: Zeff, Aeff, Zeff(E), Neff, and I are effective/descriptive quantities, not independent replacements for NIST XCOM attenuation coefficients. The Shielding transmission, μ/ρ, μ, HVL and TVL calculations continue to use the XCOM attenuation data directly; I in particular is a charged-particle stopping-power quantity and plays no role in any photon-attenuation calculation in this application.

9 Log–Log XCOM Interpolation

The application interpolates each interaction channel on the native XCOM energy grid in log–log space:

$$\ln y(E)=\ln y_1+(\ln y_2-\ln y_1)\frac{\ln E-\ln E_1}{\ln E_2-\ln E_1}.$$

Channels are interpolated independently and then summed. Pair-production channels are handled specially around their physical thresholds because their cross section is zero below threshold.

10 Absorption Edges & Grid Densification

An absorption edge occurs when a photon energy crosses an atomic-shell binding energy and a new photoelectric channel becomes accessible. The XCOM grid is densified around such discontinuities. Values extremely close to an edge are therefore sensitive to which side of the discontinuity is sampled.

Important: An edge is physical, not a plotting error. K-edge behavior is especially important for high-Z materials and for characteristic fluorescence analysis.

11 Linear Attenuation, HVL & TVL

The Shielding view uses

$$\mu=\left(\frac{\mu}{\rho}\right)\rho,\qquad T=e^{-\mu x}.$$
$$\mathrm{HVL}=\frac{\ln2}{\mu},\qquad \mathrm{TVL}=\frac{\ln10}{\mu}.$$

The reciprocal of μ, already introduced as the mean free path in Section 2, is reported directly in the Shielding readout alongside HVL and TVL:

$$\lambda_{\rm mfp}=\frac{1}{\mu}.$$

The readout also reports the areal mass thickness, the density-independent path length:

$$(\rho x)=\rho\,x.$$

For a target transmission T,

$$x_{\rm req}=\frac{-\ln T}{\mu}.$$

The corresponding required mass thickness follows from μ/ρ instead of μ, and the number of half- and tenth-value layers needed to reach it are:

$$(\rho x)_{\rm req}=\frac{-\ln T}{\mu/\rho}=\rho\,x_{\rm req},\qquad n_{\rm HVL}=\frac{x_{\rm req}}{\rm HVL},\qquad n_{\rm TVL}=\frac{x_{\rm req}}{\rm TVL}.$$

12 Multi-Layer Shielding & Layer Contributions

For layers with coefficients μi and normal thicknesses xi, the narrow-beam stack transmission is

$$T_{\rm stack}=\prod_i e^{-\mu_ix_i}=e^{-\sum_i\mu_ix_i}.$$

The layer contribution displayed by the application is the fraction of total optical depth:

$$A_i=\frac{\mu_ix_i}{\sum_j\mu_jx_j}\times100\%.$$

This is a normalized optical-depth contribution, not the percentage of photons physically removed by that layer alone.

13 Shield Optimization

The optimizer searches candidate multilayer stacks subject to a transmission requirement

$$T_{\rm total}\le T_{\rm target}.$$

It uses the same attenuation model as Shielding. For a stack of equal-thickness layers, the total optical depth is additive (-\ln T_{\rm total}=\sum_i\mu_ix_i), so the required thickness at fixed transmission is minimized by the material with the largest linear attenuation coefficient μ, and the required mass is minimized by the material with the largest mass attenuation coefficient μ/ρ, both evaluated at the selected photon energy. The optimizer computes this analytic best single material directly, and in parallel enumerates equal-thickness single- and multi-material candidate stacks (up to the configured layer count and thickness) so alternative combinations are shown alongside the analytic optimum. The optimum can change with photon energy because μ/ρ is energy dependent.

Scope: optimization is an attenuation-based design calculation. It is not a complete construction, dose-rate, thermal, structural, or Monte-Carlo shielding design.

14 Narrow-Beam & Broad-Beam Transport

Narrow-beam transmission counts the uncollided primary photons:

$$T_{\rm narrow}=e^{-\mu x}.$$

In broad-beam geometry, scattered photons may also reach the detector. A general buildup description is

$$T_{\rm broad}=B(E,\mu x)\,e^{-\mu x},\qquad B\ge1.$$

The application's explicit buildup control uses an approximation described in Section 25; it is not a replacement for a transport calculation or an authoritative buildup-factor library.

15 Shield 2D Geometry & Oblique Incidence

Shield 2D represents each shielding layer as a horizontally uniform slab. For a parallel ray incident at angle θ from the normal, a layer of normal thickness x has slant path

$$L=\frac{x}{\cos\theta}.$$

Therefore, for a multilayer stack in narrow-beam mode,

$$T(\theta)=\exp\!\left[-\sum_i\mu_i\frac{x_i}{\cos\theta}\right].$$

The 2D ray plot additionally tracks where each ray intersects layer boundaries and whether it reaches the detector. Air gaps add geometric distance but no attenuation when their attenuation coefficient is treated as negligible.

16 Beam Profiles & Source Geometry

Shield 2D supports three source profiles:

  • Uniform: parallel rays are distributed evenly across the source spread.
  • Gaussian: ray intensity is weighted by a Gaussian profile across the source spread.
  • Point source: rays diverge from a source point; the standoff distance controls the geometric divergence.

These options describe the incident beam geometry and weighting. They do not constitute a full wave-optics or radiation-transport solution.

17 Detector Geometry, Detection & Response

The detector can be represented as a point or finite-width strip. A strip centered at x_d with width W_d accepts a ray when

$$|x_{\rm hit}-x_d|\le\frac{W_d}{2}.$$

The strip detector can be sampled with multiple bins. Consequently, Shield 2D separates photon survival through the shield from geometric acceptance by the detector.

Shield 3D detector response. Beyond narrow/broad-beam transmission, the Shield 3D detector card converts the transmitted beam into detector-response quantities. The photon fluence rate reaching the detector is

$$\dot\Phi=\dot\Phi_0\,T\,f_{\rm hit},$$

where Φ̇0 is the source intensity (entered directly as a fluence rate, or as an emission rate divided by the detector area), T is the narrow/broad-beam transmission through the shield stack (Sections 11 and 14), and fhit is the fraction of traced rays that geometrically intercept the detector. The corresponding energy fluence rate uses the photon energy E in MeV:

$$\dot\Psi=\dot\Phi\,E.$$

Air kerma rate and absorbed dose rate follow from the mass energy-absorption coefficient of air and of the detector material, respectively, using the standard MeV/g-to-gray conversion:

$$\dot K_{\rm air}=\dot\Psi\left(\frac{\mu_{\rm en}}{\rho}\right)_{\!\rm air}\!\times1.602176634\times10^{-7},\qquad \dot D=\dot\Psi\left(\frac{\mu_{\rm en}}{\rho}\right)_{\!\rm det}\!\times1.602176634\times10^{-7}.$$

The detector’s intrinsic efficiency accounts for self-absorption along the active detection path L (the entered thickness, or the diameter for cylindrical/spherical detectors), combined with a user-specified additional efficiency factor:

$$\varepsilon_{\rm int}=1-\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\mu}{\rho}\right)_{\!\rm det}\rho_{\rm det}L\right],\qquad \varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\rm int}\,\varepsilon_{\rm user}.$$

Count rate and total counts over an exposure time t are

$$\dot N=\dot\Phi\,A\,\varepsilon,\qquad N=\dot N\,t,$$

with detector area A (Section 17’s geometry). The energy deposited in the detector over time t uses the absorbed-energy fraction and the MeV-to-joule conversion:

$$Q=\dot\Psi\,A\left[1-\exp\!\left(-\left(\frac{\mu_{\rm en}}{\rho}\right)_{\!\rm det}\rho_{\rm det}L\right)\right]\times1.602176634\times10^{-13}\times t.$$
Scope: these detector-response quantities are point-estimate conversions from the narrow/broad-beam transmission model. They do not model pulse-height response, dead time, energy resolution, or a full radiation-transport/Monte-Carlo detector simulation.

18 Energy-Dependent Shielding

Because each material has an energy-dependent μ/ρ(E), transmission is also energy dependent:

$$T(z,E)=\exp\left[-\sum_{i\,\mathrm{up\ to}\,z}\mu_i(E)L_i\right].$$

The Shield 2D energy-transmission profile and 3D surface visualize this quantity over energy and depth. At the full shield depth, the curve represents the primary transmitted spectrum relative to the incident spectrum, not a complete scattered-photon spectrum.

19 Interaction-Channel Fractions

At a selected energy, the contribution of channel k is

$$f_k=\frac{(\mu/\rho)_k}{(\mu/\rho)_{\rm total}},\qquad\sum_kf_k=1.$$

Shield 2D reports these fractions separately for each layer. Pair production combines the nuclear-field and electron-field channels in the displayed fraction, matching the interface definition.

20 Secondary Radiation

Primary attenuation does not mean that all interaction products disappear from the radiation field. Compton scattering produces lower-energy photons; photoelectric absorption can produce characteristic photons; pair production can produce electrons, positrons, and subsequent annihilation photons.

Model boundary: the secondary-radiation panels are indicators derived from attenuation channels and simple kinematic reference energies. They are not a coupled photon/electron/positron transport calculation.

21 Fluorescence & K-edge Secondary Photons

When photoelectric absorption creates an inner-shell vacancy, an outer-shell electron can fill it and emit a characteristic X-ray. The emitted line energy is approximately a difference of shell binding energies:

$$E_{\rm line}\approx E_{B,\,inner}-E_{B,\,outer}.$$

Near a high-Z K-edge, photoelectric absorption can therefore create a secondary-photon field. The application flags this possibility but does not calculate fluorescence yields, complete line spectra, angular distributions, or reabsorption of each emitted line.

22 Compton Scattered Photons

The Compton kinematic reference used for the secondary indicator is

$$E'=\frac{E}{1+\dfrac{E}{m_ec^2}(1-\cos\theta)}.$$

The indicator may show a reference backscatter energy, but the application does not solve the angularly resolved multiple-scattering transport problem. A full treatment would require sampling interaction locations, scattering angles, energy changes, and subsequent histories.

23 Pair Production & 511-keV Annihilation

Above 1.022 MeV, pair production can generate an electron and positron. After losing kinetic energy, the positron can annihilate with an electron. In the simplest two-photon annihilation channel, each photon has

$$E=m_ec^2\approx511\ {\rm keV}.$$

The Shield 2D indicator uses 511 keV as the characteristic annihilation reference energy. It does not transport the positron or calculate annihilation angular correlations.

24 Layer Order & Secondary Transport

For a purely narrow-beam Beer–Lambert calculation at one fixed energy,

$$T=\exp\left[-\sum_i\mu_ix_i\right],$$

so rearranging the same layers does not change the mathematical primary transmission. In a real broad-beam problem, however, order can matter because scattered photons, fluorescence photons, and other secondaries produced in an upstream layer may be absorbed or transmitted differently by downstream layers.

Interpretation: layer-order comparisons based only on primary attenuation should not be interpreted as a full secondary-radiation optimization.

25 Buildup Approximation

The broad-beam option uses the application's shared illustrative buildup-factor model rather than a Monte Carlo solution. The implemented approximation has the form

$$B(x)=1+(B_1-1)\frac{K^x-1}{K-1},$$

where x is the optical depth in mean free paths, x=μ·(\text{physical thickness}), accumulated down to the current depth in the stack. B1 and K are the two shape parameters of the approximation: B1 sets the buildup factor’s initial slope with optical depth, and K sets the rate at which that growth compounds with depth. Both are given a smooth, weak dependence on photon energy E (in keV) so that buildup is larger at lower energy, where Compton-scattered photons are more likely to reach the detector, and smaller at higher energy:

$$B_1(E)=1.08+0.28\,e^{-E_{\rm keV}/350},\qquad K(E)=1.035+0.045\,e^{-E_{\rm keV}/250}.$$

with the corresponding limiting form when K=1. The resulting broad-beam response is represented as

$$T_{\rm broad}=B\,e^{-\mu x}.$$
Important: this is an application-level approximation for visualization and comparison. It is not a tabulated ANSI/ANS, Berger, or Monte-Carlo buildup solution and should not be used as a certified shielding-design factor.

26 NIST Table 4: μ/ρ and μen/ρ

NIST SRD 126 Table 4 provides directly tabulated values for selected compounds and mixtures. The two principal quantities are the mass attenuation coefficient, μ/ρ, and the mass energy-absorption coefficient, μen/ρ.

μ/ρ describes photon attenuation from interaction removal from the primary beam. μen/ρ is an energy-absorption quantity that accounts for the fraction of photon energy ultimately transferred locally after accounting for radiative losses. They are therefore not interchangeable.

The bundled Table 4 interface preserves the directly tabulated values. Its dataset is separate from the elemental XCOM Explorer interpolation grid, so users should use the Table 4 selection when they specifically need the tabulated compound/mixture attenuation and energy-absorption coefficients.

27 Edges Detection Algorithm

The Edges view scans consecutive points of the tabulated photoelectric cross section σpe(E) for each element. A true absorption edge appears in the XCOM grid as two adjacent, near-duplicate energy points straddling the discontinuity (energy ratio between them under 1%), with the photoelectric value jumping by a wide margin between them:

$$\frac{E_{i+1}}{E_i}<1.01,\qquad \frac{\sigma_{{\rm pe},i+1}}{\sigma_{{\rm pe},i}}\ge1.3\ \text{or}\le\frac{1}{1.3}.$$

A pair of points meeting both conditions is reported as a candidate edge at their midpoint energy. This 30%-jump threshold is a practical cutoff for flagging genuine discontinuities rather than ordinary grid-to-grid variation; it is not itself a physical constant. The shell label (K/L/M) is then assigned heuristically by ordering the detected edges from highest to lowest energy and labeling them in that order — it reflects typical shell ordering, not an identification against a binding-energy table, and is therefore illustrative.

A detected row can be used to open the corresponding element in Explorer. The edge finder is a navigation and analysis aid; it is not a substitute for an authoritative atomic binding-energy reference.

28 Limitations of the Model

  • XCOM attenuation data describe photon interaction probabilities, not a complete coupled radiation-transport solution.
  • Shielding and primary Shield 2D transmission are based on Beer–Lambert attenuation of the uncollided beam.
  • Secondary-radiation indicators do not calculate electron/positron transport, fluorescence yields, complete spectra, angular distributions, or dose deposition.
  • The broad-beam buildup option is an application approximation, not a validated transport library.
  • Mixture presets are representative compositions, not certified material assays.
  • Near-edge behavior is intrinsically discontinuous and sensitive to the sampled side of the edge.
  • Optimization results are attenuation-based candidates and do not include structural, thermal, cost, regulatory, or construction constraints.

29 References & Data Provenance

  • M. J. Berger and J. H. Hubbell, XCOM: Photon Cross Sections Database, NIST Standard Reference Database 8.
  • J. H. Hubbell and S. M. Seltzer, Tables of X-Ray Mass Attenuation Coefficients and Mass Energy-Absorption Coefficients, NIST Standard Reference Database 126.
  • J. H. Scofield, relativistic Hartree–Slater photoelectric cross sections used as the basis for the XCOM photoelectric values.
  • O. Klein and Y. Nishina, Compton-scattering theory underlying the free-electron limit.
  • H. A. Bethe and W. Heitler, pair-production theory in nuclear and atomic-electron Coulomb fields.
  • Bundled application dataset: the HTML contains a compressed, client-side copy of the tabulated data; it does not query NIST at runtime.
  • ICRU Report 44: source for representative reference compositions used by selected mixture presets.
  • ICRU Report 37, Stopping Powers for Electrons and Positrons, International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements (1984): source of the recommended elemental mean excitation energies Ii, bundled directly in this application's ELEMENT_MEAN_EXCITATION_EV data table (see §8). These are charged-particle stopping-power values — unrelated to, and not derived from, the photon (x-ray/gamma) cross-section data (XCOM/SRD-8, SRD-126) that the rest of this application uses; NIST's ESTAR/ASTAR/PSTAR databases are the standard place these same ICRU-37 values are also published, for electron/proton/alpha stopping-power work unrelated to this tool.

The application's numerical implementation and bundled dataset remain the authoritative description of what is calculated in this page.

2 What This Tool Does

XCOM · Photon Cross-Section Explorer is a client-side photon attenuation and shielding exploration tool. It combines bundled NIST XCOM data with material, shielding, multilayer, geometric-ray, comparison, edge-detection, and NIST Table 4 interfaces.

Use Explorer for cross-section inspection, Shielding for one-dimensional attenuation and shield design, Shield 2D for geometric ray visualization, Compare for side-by-side materials, Edges for absorption-edge lookup, Theory for the physical basis, and Manual for control-by-control instructions.

3 The Seven Views

📊 Explorer

Inspect μ/ρ and its interaction-channel components versus photon energy for elements, compounds, mixtures, and NIST Table 4 materials.

🛡 Shielding

Calculate μ, transmission, HVL, TVL, required thickness, multilayer attenuation, buildup indicators, secondary-radiation indicators, and optimization results.

📐 Shield 2D

Trace finite-width or point-source photon rays through a multilayer slab geometry toward a point or strip detector.

📈 Compare

Compare up to the supported number of materials on a common energy-dependent plot and in numerical readouts.

⚡ Edges

Search for elements near a target absorption edge and inspect detected edge candidates.

📚 Theory

Read the physics, equations, geometry, secondary-radiation scope, NIST Table 4 definitions, algorithms, and model limitations.

📝 Manual

Use this page as the practical guide to every major control and result panel.

Switch between views with the buttons at the top. Each view maintains its own controls and state while you navigate.

4 Material Selection

Explorer provides four material modes:

Element

Select an element from the periodic-table grid.

Compound

Enter an XCOM-style formula or choose a preset. Parentheses, dots, and spaces are not accepted by the formula parser.

Mixture

Add formula/weight-fraction components. Weights are normalized automatically.

NIST Table 4

Select one of the directly tabulated compounds/mixtures from the bundled SRD 126 Table 4 dataset.

5 Energy Range & Probe

  1. Set the minimum and maximum plotted energy and choose eV, keV, MeV, or GeV.
  2. Optionally enter density to obtain linear attenuation quantities in the Explorer probe.
  3. Enter a probe energy to read total and channel-specific attenuation values.

The Explorer elemental dataset is limited to its supported XCOM range of 1 keV–100 GeV.

6 Chart Controls & Series

  • X-axis / Y-axis: choose log or linear scaling.
  • Markers: show or hide sampled points.
  • Series: toggle total and individual interaction channels.
  • Autoscale: reset chart zoom and scaling.

7 Data Table & CSV Export

The sampled data table reports energy and the available attenuation channels. Use Export CSV to save the sampled curve for external analysis.

8 NIST Table 4

Select NIST Table 4 in Explorer to work with directly tabulated compound/mixture data from NIST SRD 126. The Table 4 view displays both

$$\frac{\mu}{\rho}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\mu_{\rm en}}{\rho}.$$

Use μ/ρ for attenuation and μen/ρ when the question concerns energy absorption. Do not treat the two quantities as interchangeable.

9 Material, Density & Photon Energy

  1. Select the shielding material using Element, Compound, or Mixture.
  2. Enter density in g/cm³.
  3. Enter photon energy and unit.
  4. Read the material parameters panel for μ/ρ, μ, transmission-related quantities, HVL, and TVL.

10 Material Parameters

The Material parameters card updates automatically when the material, density, photon energy, or energy unit changes. It reports attenuation quantities together with the material descriptors Zeff, Aeff, Zeff(E), and the mean excitation energy I (from Bragg's additivity rule over the material's elemental composition).

  • Zeff: composition-only effective atomic number using the electron-fraction Z2.94 convention.
  • Aeff: electron-fraction-weighted effective atomic mass.
  • Zeff(E): energy-dependent effective atomic number calculated from the elemental XCOM μ/ρ(E) contributions at the current photon energy.
  • μ/ρ: mass attenuation coefficient; μ = ρ(μ/ρ) is the linear attenuation coefficient.
  • HVL and TVL follow from the current μ.
$$Z_{\rm eff}(E)=\left[\sum_i q_i(E)Z_i^{2.94}\right]^{1/2.94},\quad q_i(E)=\frac{w_i[\mu/\rho]_i(E)}{\sum_j w_j[\mu/\rho]_j(E)}.$$

Tip: change the photon energy and observe Zeff(E). Zeff and Aeff do not change with energy because they describe composition; Zeff(E) does because its weights come from energy-dependent XCOM attenuation.

For water, the composition-only value is approximately Zeff = 7.42 under this convention. Zeff(E) is a separate energy-dependent descriptor and should not be confused with the fixed composition value.

11 Shield Thickness & Target Transmission

Enter a shield thickness in mm, cm, or m. The target-transmission field specifies the maximum desired percentage. The required-thickness panel inverts Beer–Lambert to find the thickness corresponding to that target.

11 Material Comparison

Add reference materials to compare density, μ/ρ, μ, HVL, TVL, and the thickness needed for 1% transmission. Comparison is energy dependent, so change the photon energy to see how the ranking changes.

12 Multi-Layer Shielding

Build a source-to-detector stack. Each layer can have its own material, thickness, density, and enabled air gap. The narrow-beam primary transmission is calculated layer by layer and combined multiplicatively.

$$T_{\rm stack}=\exp\left(-\sum_i\mu_ix_i\right).$$

13 Layer Contribution Analysis

The contribution display shows the fraction of total optical depth supplied by each layer:

$$A_i=\frac{\mu_ix_i}{\sum_j\mu_jx_j}\times100\%.$$

A large contribution means a large share of the stack's optical depth; it does not mean that exactly that percentage of all incident photons is removed by that layer alone.

14 Radiation Buildup

Use the narrow/broad-beam control to compare the uncollided primary result with the application's approximate buildup response. Narrow beam uses B=1; broad beam applies the shared approximation documented in Theory Section 25.

15 Secondary Radiation / K-edge

The Secondary Radiation / K-edge panel indicates when a high-Z layer and the selected energy are near a possible K-edge. It separates primary attenuation from possible secondary-photon mechanisms such as fluorescence, Compton scattering, and pair-production products.

Important: the panel is an indicator, not a full secondary-radiation transport calculation.

16 Shield Optimization

Set the target transmission, available materials, maximum total thickness, and maximum number of layers. Select the objective (minimum thickness or minimum mass) and inspect the ranked feasible stacks.

17 Layer-Order Comparison

Use the order-comparison controls to test different sequences of the same shielding materials. For fixed-energy narrow-beam Beer–Lambert attenuation, rearranging layers does not change primary transmission because the optical depths add. Any real order dependence is a secondary-transport effect.

18 Layer Geometry

In Shield 2D, layers are horizontal slabs. The geometry view shows their boundaries, thicknesses, material labels, source region, photon paths, and detector position. For an oblique parallel ray, the path through a layer is x/cosθ.

19 Photon Tracking

The ray display follows individual geometric photon paths through the stack. Ray brightness represents surviving primary intensity in the visualization. Rays that do not land inside the detector acceptance are shown separately from detector hits.

20 Beam & Geometry

Set photon energy, beam angle, number of photons, source lateral spread, and beam profile. Choose Uniform, Gaussian, or Point source. Narrow beam uses pure Beer–Lambert attenuation; broad beam applies the application's buildup approximation.

21 Detector

Set detector lateral position and width. Choose Point or Strip. A strip detector can be sampled with configurable bins across its width.

22 Shield Layers

Add layers in source-to-detector order. Each layer has material, thickness, and density override. Air gaps can be inserted after layers. Oblique rays use the longer slant path through each slab.

23 2D Ray Geometry

The ray plot shows source points, photon trajectories, layer boundaries, the detector, and detector misses/hits. Use Play to animate the ray traversal and Reset to restore the initial geometry.

24 2D Intensity Field

The intensity field displays I(x,z)/I0 through the illuminated region. Choose linear/log color scaling, standard/fine grid resolution, and contour visibility. Unlit regions are geometric shadow regions, not a calculation of scattered dose.

25 Depth Intensity Profile

The depth profile shows primary transmission along the beam centerline versus depth. Linear/log Y scaling is available, with HVL and TVL crossing markers and layer-boundary markers.

26 Energy Transmission Profile

Choose a depth and plot I/I0(E). Setting the depth to the total shield depth gives the primary transmitted-energy dependence of the complete stack.

27 Energy-Dependent 3D Shielding

The 3D surface uses depth on one axis, photon energy on the other, and I/I0 vertically. Set energy limits, log/linear energy scale, global/local extrema, and the number of energy points.

28 Interaction-Channel Fractions

The table reports photoelectric, Compton, coherent, and pair-production fractions for every layer at the selected energy. The displayed fractions sum to 100% for each valid layer.

29 Secondary Radiation Indicator

The indicator separates transmitted primary photons from possible scattered photons, fluorescence photons, annihilation photons, and pair-production secondaries. The listed secondary energies are reference/indicative energies, not transported spectra.

30 Compare

Use the dedicated Compare view to add the supported number of materials and compare their attenuation curves on a common energy axis. Use this view when the question is “which material attenuates more strongly over this energy range?” rather than “what thickness do I need?”

31 Edges

Enter a target energy and tolerance to search the bundled elemental data for nearby absorption-edge candidates. The results table reports element, Z, and detected edges. Click a row to open the corresponding element in Explorer.

Shell labels are heuristic and illustrative; use an authoritative binding-energy reference for exact atomic-edge assignments.

32 Theory & Limitations

The Theory tab is the physics reference for this Manual. In particular, read Sections 14–24 before interpreting Shield 2D, broad-beam buildup, secondary-radiation indicators, or layer-order results.

  • The application does not perform full Monte Carlo photon/electron transport.
  • Primary attenuation is Beer–Lambert based.
  • Secondary-radiation panels are indicators rather than complete transport calculations.
  • Near absorption edges, small energy changes can produce genuine discontinuities.
  • Mixture presets are representative compositions.
  • Optimization is an attenuation-based engineering calculation, not a complete shielding design certification.
Recommended workflow: Explorer/Compare → inspect energy dependence → Shielding → build layers → inspect contributions/buildup/secondary indicators → use Shield 2D to inspect geometry and detector acceptance → consult authoritative transport/shielding methods for final engineering decisions.
